To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the sensitivity of human dermal tissue to the presence of anemia is higher for the wavelengths in the near-infrared range than for the wavelengths in both the visible and ultraviolet ranges.

(1) the spectral sensitivity of human skin is strongly influenced by the anemia severity level, (2) the skin's spectral response to anemia is highly dependent on the type of skin tissue, and (3) the proposed monitoring procedure, which relies on the use of a hyperspectral camera and a simple mathematical model, is capable of accurately estimating the severity level of anemia in skin tissues.

“The spectral responses of human skin to reduced hemoglobin levels, associated with increasing anemic severity levels, are sensitive to the biophysical and morphologic characteristics of the tissue, but the sensitivity of the responses is not affected by the severity of the anemia.”
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and validation of a new tool to be used in the early detection and follow-up of anemic individuals.
the assessment of the potential of hyperspectral responses to detect and monitor the severity levels of anemia.
the development and validation of an innovative approach to the study of the optical properties of skin tissue in anemia.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the spectral signatures of human skin are sensitive to anemia, and the hyperspectral response of this tissue may be used to monitor the severity level of this disease.
the sensitivity of the hyperspectral response of human skin is not uniform, and the spectral regions of maximum sensitivity vary with the skin specimen under study.
the hyperspectral responses of skin are sensitive to the effects of anemia, but the sensitivity of these responses is not the same for all the spectral regions and for all the skin types.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the spectral signatures associated with the anemic condition are not only detectable but also quantifiable, which opens the possibility for the development of low-cost, noninvasive, and risk-free optical devices for its monitoring.
the hyperspectral response of human skin is sensitive enough to the changes in hemoglobin concentrations associated to anemia to be considered a potential indicator of this disorder.

the hyperspectral responses of skin specimens can be used as a reliable indicator of anemia severity, and this property can be exploited in the development of noninvasive, low-cost, portable diagnostic devices for this disorder.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the hyperspectral responses of the skin can be effectively used for the assessment of the anemic condition and its severity levels.
the hyperspectral responses of human skin to anemia are highly sensitive to changes in its severity level and, thus, can be used as a reliable and low-cost diagnostic tool.
the spectral reflectance of human skin is sensitive to anemia, and that the sensitivity of the reflectance spectra of different skin types to anemia severity varies significantly.
